title: Three Ways to Answer One Question: What Is It Worth?
summary: Value is an opinion about a price that has not happened yet. Appraisers reach it three ways: what the property earns, what similar properties sold for, and what it would cost to build again. Knowing where each method bends lets you read any appraisal and see which number is doing the work.
body:
Mr Shabazz, value is an opinion about a price that has not happened yet. It is reached three ways — what the property earns, what similar properties sold for, and what it would cost to build again — and each way bends in a predictable place.

Recall

Q. From the returns week: what is after-tax leakage?

A. The gap between the return a pre-tax model shows and the return that actually reaches the owner once taxes at the entity level and the personal level have been paid. A deal can look strong before tax and ordinary after it.

Q. From the second pro forma week: what is stabilised net operating income?

A. Net operating income (NOI) is rent and other income, less vacancy and operating expenses, before debt payments and before income tax. Stabilised means measured after lease-up, once occupancy has settled at a level the building can sustain.

Q. From the week on protecting the base: why does a will belong in a course on wealth?

A. Because it decides who receives your assets and who acts for your estate. Without one, rules you did not choose make those decisions, and value leaks through delay and dispute.

Why this matters

Almost every money decision in development passes through a valuation. A lender sizes your loan on an appraised value. Investors decide how much equity to commit based on what the finished building will be worth. You buy land on a seller's view of value and sell the building on a buyer's view. If you cannot read a valuation critically, you are letting someone else's opinion set your leverage, your equity and your exit. The goal of this lesson is not to make you an appraiser. It is to make you the person in the room who can see which of three numbers is carrying the conclusion.

The income approach: what it earns

Plain English first. An income property is a machine that produces cash. A buyer pays for the machine based on what it produces and how risky that stream looks.

The professional framing has two versions. Direct capitalisation takes one year of stabilised NOI and divides it by a capitalisation rate, or cap rate: the yield that buyers in the current market accept for this kind of property. Value equals NOI divided by cap rate. The second version is the discounted cash flow (DCF): project the cash flows year by year, add a sale price at the end, and discount everything back to today at a rate that reflects risk.

Worked example, hypothetical round numbers. A finished apartment building is expected to produce stabilised NOI of $600,000 a year. Recent sales suggest buyers accept a 6.0 percent cap rate. Value is $600,000 divided by 0.06, which is $10,000,000. Now move the cap rate half a point to 6.5 percent. Value becomes $600,000 divided by 0.065, about $9,230,000. Half a point of opinion moved value by roughly $770,000. That is where the income approach bends: in the choice of cap rate, and in whether the NOI has been honestly normalised — vacancy included, management fee included, reserves for replacing roofs and equipment included.

The sales comparison approach: what similar things sold for

Plain English: look at what buyers actually paid for similar properties, then adjust for the differences.

The professional framing: the appraiser selects comparable sales, called comparables or comps, converts each to a unit of comparison such as price per apartment or price per square foot, and adjusts each comp for differences in location, size, age, condition, date of sale and the terms of the deal. A sale with seller financing or a forced sale is not a clean comp.

Worked example. Three hypothetical sales of similar 40-unit buildings sold at $260,000, $240,000 and $250,000 per unit. Your building is newer than the second comp and in a weaker location than the first. After adjustments the appraiser lands at $250,000 per unit, so 40 units suggest $10,000,000. Where it bends: in thin markets there may be no true comps, and every adjustment is a judgement. Five adjustments of 4 percent each, all in one direction, quietly add 20 percent.

Say that out loud now.

The cost approach: what it would cost to build again

Plain English: a rational buyer will not pay more for an existing building than it would cost to buy land and build an equivalent one.

The professional framing: land value, plus the replacement cost of the building as new, less depreciation for physical wear and for features the market no longer wants, plus an allowance for the profit a developer would need to take the risk. That allowance is often called entrepreneurial incentive. The method is strongest for new buildings and special-purpose buildings, and weakest for old ones, where depreciation becomes a guess.

Worked example. Land is worth $2,000,000. Building the same 40 units new would cost $7,500,000 in hard and soft costs. A developer would want $500,000 of incentive to take the risk. The cost approach suggests $10,000,000 for a brand-new building. For a 20-year-old building you would subtract depreciation, and the answer becomes softer with every year of age.

Reconciliation, and why the three must be read together

The appraiser does not average the three numbers. The final step, called reconciliation, weighs each approach according to how reliable its evidence is for this property. For a stabilised apartment building with good rent data, the income approach usually carries most of the weight. For a vacant new building, the cost approach may matter more.

Here is the developer's insight. The gap between the income approach and the cost approach is the reason development happens at all. When a building is worth more than it costs to build, someone builds. When it is worth less, nobody does, and the land waits. That is the development spread from the value week, seen from the appraiser's chair. When you read an appraisal, put the income value and the cost value side by side. If the income value is far above cost, ask why others are not building. If it is below cost, ask why you are.

How the best do it

Large institutional owners of real estate generally treat valuation as a control, not a sales tool. The common practices are these: they commission external valuations on a regular cycle, they rotate valuers so no single opinion becomes a habit, they separate the people who report value from the people whose pay depends on it, and they compare past appraised values with the prices properties actually sold for. A small developer can copy all four at almost no cost. Get an independent opinion at each major decision gate, never let the person who wants the deal approve its value, and keep a simple log of every value you estimated next to the price that later happened.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is choosing the approach that gives the number you want. A developer who likes the income approach because it produces the highest figure is not valuing the building, he is decorating his hope. The control is to run all three, write down which one you trust most and why before you look at the results, and explain any gap larger than about 10 percent between them. That 10 percent is a practitioner habit, not a standard; set your own threshold and keep it. Professional sign-off required: a licensed or designated appraiser.

The beginner's mistake

Treating the cap rate as a fact you look up. A cap rate is an opinion drawn from a handful of recent sales, each with its own story. Always ask for the range, the specific sales behind it, and how old they are. The second beginner's mistake is treating appraised value as money. An appraisal is not cash; it is a reason for a lender to lend and a buyer to pay, and both can change their minds.

Callback

In the value week you learned the development spread: yield on cost compared with the market cap rate. This lesson shows you where both of those numbers come from. Yield on cost comes from your own pro forma. The market cap rate comes from the income approach, and the appraiser's comps are the evidence behind it. The spread is only as reliable as the weakest of those two sources.

Recap

Value is reached three ways. The income approach asks what the building earns and bends at the cap rate. The sales comparison approach asks what similar buildings sold for and bends at the adjustments. The cost approach asks what it would cost to build again and bends at depreciation. Read the three together, and the gap between income value and cost is the reason to build or not.

Next: Ford, on a famous deal where the price was set by a plan rather than by the building.
checklist: Ask for all three approaches, even if one carries most of the weight.
Write down which approach you trust most and why before you see the results.
Ask for the cap rate range and the specific sales behind it, with dates.
Check that NOI includes vacancy, a management fee and replacement reserves.
Count the adjustments on each comparable sale and note their direction.
Put income value next to cost value and explain the gap.
Log every value you estimate so you can compare it with what later happens.
head: Field checklist
speak: An appraisal answers one question three ways. The income approach asks what the building earns: stabilised net operating income divided by a cap rate, or a discounted cash flow. It bends at the cap rate; half a point moves value by close to ten percent. The sales comparison approach asks what similar buildings sold for, adjusted for differences. It bends at the adjustments, which are judgements. The cost approach asks what it would cost to buy land and build again, less depreciation, plus a developer's incentive. It bends at depreciation, so it suits new buildings best. The appraiser reconciles the three by weighing the evidence, not by averaging. The developer's insight is the gap between income value and cost: when value is above cost, people build. My rule is to run all three, decide which I trust before I see the numbers, and explain any big gap between them.
terms: Capitalisation rate — the yield buyers currently accept for a type of property, used to turn one year of net operating income into a value.
Comparable sale — a recent sale of a similar property, adjusted for differences, used as evidence of value.
Reconciliation — the appraiser's final step of weighing the three approaches by the reliability of their evidence, rather than averaging them.

hostile.q: Your valuation rests almost entirely on the income approach. Why should I ignore the cost approach, which says this building is worth less?
hostile.a: You should not ignore it, and I have not. The income approach carries most of the weight because we have twelve months of rent evidence from comparable buildings and recent sales to support the cap rate. The cost approach is lower because it includes a conservative depreciation allowance. I have reconciled the gap in writing, and if you want to underwrite to the lower figure, I can show you what the deal looks like there.

title: Stuyvesant Town: When the Price Was Set by the Plan, Not the Building
summary: In 2006 a large Manhattan apartment complex sold for a price that only worked if rents rose much faster than the existing rules allowed. Taken through seven forensic steps, the case shows how a valuation built on a future plan becomes a liability when the plan meets the law. The prevention rule: value what exists under today's rules first.
body:
Mr Shabazz, the most dangerous number in real estate is a value that depends on a future nobody has yet been permitted to build. Stuyvesant Town is the clearest public example of that danger, and Roman sits beside me today to read it from the lender's chair.

Recall

Q. From the returns week: what is one IRR trap?

A. The internal rate of return (IRR) can rank a small, quick deal above a larger one that creates far more wealth, because it measures speed of return rather than amount. Read it beside the equity multiple.

Q. From the second pro forma week: what is absorption?

A. The pace at which the market takes up new space — units leased or sold per month. It sets how long you carry costs before income stabilises.

Q. From the week on protecting the base: what is an emergency reserve for?

A. To keep you from being forced to sell or borrow on bad terms when something goes wrong. It buys time, and time is what a forced seller does not have.

Why this matters

Every development is valued partly on a future: the building that will exist, the rents it will earn. That is unavoidable. The failure in this case was letting the price, and the debt, rest on a future that the existing legal framework did not yet permit. You will meet the small version of this every year: land priced on a rezoning not yet granted, a building priced on rents not yet achieved. The facts below come from the public record; verify the specifics against primary sources before you cite them in a meeting.

Step 1: Timeline

In 2006 MetLife sold Stuyvesant Town and Peter Cooper Village, two adjoining complexes in Manhattan with roughly 11,000 apartments, to a partnership of Tishman Speyer and BlackRock for about $5.4 billion. Most of the apartments were rent-stabilised, which under New York's rules limits how much rent can rise for existing tenants. The purchase was financed largely with senior and mezzanine debt. In October 2009 New York's highest court ruled in a tenants' case that apartments in buildings receiving a particular property tax benefit could not be deregulated while the benefit applied. In January 2010 the owners defaulted and handed the property to their lenders.

Step 2: Key decisions

The decisive choice was the price itself, set on a plan to convert rent-stabilised apartments to market rents as tenants moved out. The second decision was the capital structure: a high proportion of debt, with reserves set aside to cover the gap between what the buildings earned and what the debt cost while the conversion happened. The third was the pace assumed for that conversion.

Step 3: Assumptions

The price assumed three things at once. That the regulatory path to market rents was open. That turnover would happen fast enough. And that market rents would hold. Each was plausible alone. Together, they made the value of the deal a forecast of the as-stabilised value rather than the as-is value — the difference you learn this week.

Say that out loud now.

Step 4: Incentives

Roman's view from the lender's chair: in 2006 credit was abundant, and the fees on arranging and selling large loans rewarded volume. Mezzanine lenders were paid for taking the risk of a thin margin of value above the senior loan. The equity sponsors were competing in an auction for a landmark asset. A seller running an auction is paid to find the most optimistic buyer, not the most accurate one. When every party is paid on the transaction closing, nobody is paid to say the value is wrong.

Step 5: Warning signs ignored

The plan required a change in tenant status across thousands of homes in a city where tenant protection is politically strong. Tenant groups were organised and vocal. The income at purchase covered only part of the debt service, which meant the deal depended on reserves from the first day. When a deal cannot pay its own debt as it stands, the reserves are not a cushion; they are a countdown clock.

Step 6: Point of no return

The point of no return was the closing itself, because the capital structure left no room to wait. Once the reserves were sized to a timeline, any delay — slower turnover, a court decision, a weaker rental market after 2008 — consumed them. By the time the court ruled in 2009, the market had already fallen and the reserves were running down. The ruling did not create the failure; it removed the last path out.

Step 7: Root cause

The root cause was a valuation that treated a permitted future as if it were a present fact, financed with debt that had no tolerance for delay. The appraised and transaction value captured upside that depended on regulation and tenant behaviour, and the debt was sized to that upside. When the future arrived late and different, the gap between the as-is value and the price became a loss that fell first on the equity and then on the junior lenders.

The pattern in small numbers

Here is the same shape at a scale you will meet, in hypothetical round numbers. A building earns NOI of $700,000 today. At a 7.0 percent cap rate its as-is value is $10,000,000. The business plan says that after converting units, NOI will reach $1,120,000, and at the same cap rate the as-stabilised value would be $16,000,000. A lender advances 75 percent of the as-stabilised figure, $12,000,000 — already $2,000,000 more than the building is worth today. That gap is the first warning.

Second example. Debt service on $12,000,000 is, say, $1,000,000 a year. The building earns $700,000, so the shortfall is $300,000 a year, and the sponsor funds a $900,000 reserve: three years at plan. If conversion arrives at half the planned pace, the shortfall shrinks more slowly, and the reserve runs out while NOI is still far below $1,000,000. Nothing dramatic has to happen. Slow is enough.

The biggest risk

The risk for you is buying or lending on value that depends on a change you do not control: a rezoning, a deregulation, a new road, a tenant leaving. The control is to separate value into two lines in every memo: the value of what exists under today's rules, and the additional value that depends on a future event. Finance the first with debt if you must. Finance the second with equity and with time, and size your reserves to the slow case, not the plan.

The beginner's mistake

Reading a reserve as safety. A reserve set aside because the building cannot pay its debt is evidence that the deal does not work today. The beginner sees a large interest reserve and feels protected. The professional asks how many months it lasts if every assumption arrives a year late.

Callback

In the pro forma weeks you learned to build stabilised NOI after lease-up and absorption. Stuyvesant Town shows what happens when stabilised NOI is used as if it had already arrived. The stabilised line in a pro forma is a destination, not a starting point, and the road to it has a cost that must be in the budget.

Recap

Seven steps: a 2006 purchase priced on converting regulated rents; heavy debt with reserves to cover the shortfall; assumptions about law, turnover and rents that all had to hold; incentives that rewarded closing; warning signs from tenants and from day-one cash flow; a point of no return at closing; and a root cause of financing a future as if it were the present. A different buyer later acquired the complex in 2015, on terms that included commitments on affordable housing, which shows the asset was never worthless. The problem was the price and the debt, not the building.

Next: Priya, on how one appraised number moves your loan, your equity and your return.
checklist: Split every valuation into today's-rules value and future-event value.
Ask what legal or regulatory change the price depends on, and who controls it.
Check whether the property pays its own debt service on day one.
Size reserves to the slow case, not the business plan.
Map who is paid on closing and who is paid on accuracy.
Identify the point after which you cannot wait, and plan before it.
Read tenant, community and political signals as risk inputs, not noise.
head: Field checklist
rule: Rule 16: Value what exists under today's rules first; any value that depends on a future change must be financed with equity and time, never borrowed against as if it were already earned.
speak: Stuyvesant Town sold in 2006 for about five point four billion dollars, financed mostly with debt. The price depended on converting rent-stabilised apartments to market rents as tenants left. The deal could not cover its debt from day one, so reserves filled the gap. That made the reserves a countdown clock. The market fell after 2008, and in 2009 New York's highest court ruled that units in buildings receiving a particular tax benefit could not be deregulated. In January 2010 the owners handed the property to the lenders. The root cause was treating a future that the rules had not yet allowed as a present fact, and sizing the debt to it. Rule 16: value what exists under today's rules first, and finance any future upside with equity and time, never with debt sized as if it were already earned.
terms: As-is value — the value of a property in its current physical and legal condition on the valuation date.
As-stabilised value — a forward-looking value assuming the property has reached sustainable occupancy and income.
Mezzanine debt — a loan ranking behind the senior mortgage, usually secured by the ownership interests, that takes more risk for a higher return.

hostile.q: Your projected value assumes a rezoning that has not been approved. Why should I lend against it?
hostile.a: You should not, and I am not asking you to. The loan request is sized to the as-is value under the current zoning. The rezoning upside is shown as a separate line, funded with equity, and the reserves are sized for a twelve-month delay beyond our planning estimate. If the rezoning fails, the project still services its debt.

title: One Appraised Number Moves Your Loan, Your Equity and Your Return
summary: A lender sizes your loan partly on appraised value, so the appraisal decides how much equity you must find and what return that equity earns. A modest gap in value turns into a much larger gap in equity and return. This lesson works the arithmetic and ends with what valuation means for your personal balance sheet.
body:
Mr Shabazz, a valuation is not a report you file. It is an input that sets your loan, and the loan sets how much equity you must find and what that equity earns. A small change in value becomes a large change in your return.

Recall

Q. From the returns week: what is the equity multiple?

A. Total cash returned to the equity investors divided by the cash they put in. A multiple of 1.5 means every dollar came back as a dollar fifty. Unlike IRR, it ignores time.

Q. From the second pro forma week: what is vacancy and credit loss?

A. The allowance for space that sits empty and rent that is billed but never collected. It is deducted from potential gross income to reach effective gross income.

Q. From the week on protecting the base: what is the job of insurance in a wealth plan?

A. To move a loss you could not survive onto someone who is paid to carry it, so that one event does not undo years of building.

Why this matters

You will raise equity from yourself or from partners, and equity is the most expensive money in the deal. Every dollar the lender will not advance is a dollar of equity you must find, and every extra dollar of equity dilutes the return on all the others. Lenders size loans to more than one test at once, and value is usually one of them. So the appraiser, whom you do not control, has a direct hand on your return.

Two tests, one loan

Plain English: a construction lender will lend you the smaller of two amounts — a share of what the project costs, and a share of what it will be worth.

The professional framing: loan-to-cost (LTC) is the loan divided by total project cost. Loan-to-value (LTV) is the loan divided by appraised value; for a project still to be built, lenders usually look at the as-complete or as-stabilised value. Each lender sets its own maximum for each test. These percentages are commercial practice, not standards, and they move with the credit cycle. The binding limit is whichever test produces the smaller loan.

Worked example, hypothetical. Total project cost is $10,000,000, including land. The lender will advance at most 65 percent of cost and at most 60 percent of appraised as-complete value. Your own estimate of as-complete value is $12,000,000.

  • Cost test: 65 percent of $10,000,000 is $6,500,000.
  • Value test at your estimate: 60 percent of $12,000,000 is $7,200,000.
  • The loan is the smaller, $6,500,000. Equity required is $3,500,000.

Now the appraiser concludes $10,500,000, not $12,000,000. The value test becomes 60 percent of $10,500,000, which is $6,300,000. Value now binds. The loan falls by $200,000, and your equity rises to $3,700,000. If the appraisal had come in at $10,000,000, the loan would be $6,000,000 and the equity $4,000,000 — half a million more than you planned.

Say that out loud now.

What the gap does to your return

Keep the same project and suppose you sell it on completion for $12,000,000, with a $2,000,000 profit after all costs. To keep the arithmetic clean, ignore selling costs and the small change in interest.

Appraised valueLoanEquityEquity multiple
$12,000,000$6,500,000$3,500,0001.57
$10,500,000$6,300,000$3,700,0001.54
$10,000,000$6,000,000$4,000,0001.50

The multiple is equity plus profit, divided by equity. At $3,500,000 of equity it is 5.5 divided by 3.5, or about 1.57. At $4,000,000 it is 6.0 divided by 4.0, exactly 1.50. That looks small. It is not, for two reasons. First, the half million had to come from somewhere — your pocket or a partner who will want a share of the profit for it. Second, a low appraisal is often information: if a trained valuer sees $10,000,000, the buyer you plan to sell to may see something close to it too.

Value at the exit: the cap rate hits leverage

The second place valuation moves your money is the exit. Suppose a finished building is expected to produce NOI of $700,000. At a 5.5 percent cap rate it is worth about $12,727,000. If the market moves to 6.0 percent by the time you sell, it is worth about $11,667,000. Value fell by roughly $1,060,000, about 8 percent.

But you do not own the whole building. If $3,500,000 of the capital stack is your equity, a $1,060,000 fall in value comes almost entirely out of that equity, because the lender is repaid first. An 8 percent fall in value becomes about a 30 percent fall in the value of your equity. That is what leverage does, and it works just as hard against you as for you. When you read a valuation, always translate the change in value into a change in equity.

Know your cushion before the appraiser does

Here is a calculation worth doing on every deal before you order the appraisal. Ask how far value can fall before the value test, rather than the cost test, sets your loan. In the example, the cost test gives $6,500,000. The value test gives the same amount when 60 percent of value equals $6,500,000, which is a value of $6,500,000 divided by 0.60, about $10,833,000. Your own estimate is $12,000,000. So value can fall about $1,167,000, or roughly 9.7 percent, before your equity plan changes at all. Below that, every $100,000 of lost value costs you $60,000 of loan, dollar for dollar replaced by equity. Write that cushion in your deal memo. When the appraisal arrives, you will know in ten seconds whether it matters.

Wealth Ledger

Warrick's note for your personal balance sheet. Carry real estate at an honest as-is market value, less the cost of selling and less the debt against it, not at the as-complete value in your business plan. A project under construction is worth what it would fetch half-built, which is usually far less than its cost to date. Equity that exists only in a forecast is not liquid, cannot pay a bill, and should not be counted toward your liquidity floor. A licensed adviser is required before you act on any personal financial decision.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is closing your equity plan on your own value estimate and discovering the appraisal gap at the commitment letter, when land is already bought and your equity is committed. The control is to commission an early independent valuation opinion before you buy land, to size your equity to the lower of your estimate and that opinion, and to hold a written equity reserve for the gap. Professional sign-off required: a designated appraiser for the valuation and a lender's credit team for the sizing.

The beginner's mistake

Assuming the loan is a fixed percentage of cost. Beginners model the loan as 65 percent of cost and forget that the value test, or a debt service coverage test once the building is income producing, may bind first. Always calculate every test the lender uses and let the smallest one set the loan.

Callback

In the sources and uses lesson of the first pro forma week, every dollar of use needed a source. This lesson shows how the sources side is fragile: the debt source is not a number you choose, it is a number the appraisal and the lender's tests give you. When value moves, sources and uses fall out of balance, and equity is the only line that can close the gap.

Recap

Lenders lend the smaller of a share of cost and a share of value. A low appraisal can make value the binding test, cut the loan and raise your equity. At the exit, a move in cap rate changes value, and leverage magnifies that change in your equity. On your own balance sheet, count as-is value, net of selling costs and debt.

Next: REGA, on the standards and rules that govern how an appraisal is made and who may rely on it.
checklist: List every sizing test the lender uses, and calculate each one.
Identify which test binds, and how far the others are from binding.
Get an independent valuation opinion before buying land.
Size equity to the lower of your estimate and the independent opinion.
Hold a written equity reserve for an appraisal gap.
Translate every change in value into a change in your equity.
Carry personal real estate at as-is value, net of selling costs and debt.
head: Field checklist
speak: A lender usually lends the smaller of two amounts: a share of what the project costs and a share of what it will be worth. Say cost is ten million, the lender lends sixty-five percent of cost and sixty percent of appraised value. At a twelve million appraisal, cost binds and the loan is six and a half million. If the appraisal comes in at ten million, value binds, the loan drops to six million, and I must find half a million more equity. At the exit, the cap rate moves value, and leverage magnifies it. An eight percent fall in value can be a thirty percent fall in my equity, because the lender is repaid first. So I get an independent valuation before buying land, size my equity to the lower estimate, and hold a reserve for the gap. On my own balance sheet I carry property at as-is value, net of selling costs and debt.
terms: Loan-to-cost — the loan divided by total project cost, one of the tests lenders use to size a loan.
Loan-to-value — the loan divided by appraised value, often the as-complete or as-stabilised value for a project not yet built.
Binding limit — the sizing test that produces the smallest loan and therefore sets the loan amount.

hostile.q: The appraisal came in eight percent below your number. Where is the extra equity coming from, and why should I believe your exit value now?
hostile.a: The equity gap is covered by a reserve we set aside before buying the land, sized to exactly this case, so no new money has to be raised. On the exit, I have rebased our sale value to the appraised figure, not my own, and the deal still clears our minimum return. If you want to test it further, here is the case at a further half-point increase in the cap rate.

title: The Rules Behind an Appraisal: Standards, Assumptions and Who May Rely
summary: An appraisal is governed by professional standards that define what it is for, who it is for, and which assumptions it rests on. An as-complete value is built on a stated condition that is not true today. Reading the assumptions and the intended user tells you what the number can and cannot be used for.
body:
Mr Shabazz, an appraisal is a regulated professional opinion with its own rule book. The number at the front only means something once you have read three things at the back: who it is for, what it is for, and which assumptions it treats as true.

Recall

Q. From the returns week: why can a pre-tax IRR mislead an owner?

A. Because tax falls at different times and at different levels, so two deals with the same pre-tax return can deliver very different after-tax returns. The owner keeps after-tax money.

Q. From the second pro forma week: what rules govern how a lease-up is modelled?

A. None in law; it is a modelling convention. That is why the assumptions about absorption and concessions must be written down and defended, not buried in a formula.

Q. From the week on protecting the base: what is a power of attorney?

A. A legal document appointing someone to act for you, for example if you are unable to. Its form and limits depend on local law, which you must verify with a lawyer.

Why this matters

You will hold appraisals in your hand for land, for construction loans, for refinancing and for sale. Lenders, investors and courts treat them differently depending on which standards they follow and who they were written for. A developer who waves the wrong appraisal at a lender, or relies on a value the report itself says is conditional, loses credibility in a single sentence. This lesson teaches concepts. The exact requirements depend on where you are and who the lender is; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

The standards family

Plain English: appraisers in most established markets follow a written professional code that says how an opinion of value must be developed and reported.

The professional framing: in the United States the main code is the Uniform Standards of Professional Appraisal Practice, known as USPAP, published by The Appraisal Foundation. In Canada, members of the Appraisal Institute of Canada follow the Canadian Uniform Standards of Professional Appraisal Practice. Internationally, the International Valuation Standards Council publishes the International Valuation Standards, and the Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors publishes its own global valuation standards, widely called the Red Book. Each is revised from time to time, so always verify against the current edition before you cite any requirement.

What they share, at the level of concept: the appraiser must define the problem before solving it, must be independent and unbiased, must disclose assumptions, and must report in a way that does not mislead the intended user.

What "market value" means

Plain English: market value is the most probable price a property would sell for in a fair sale between informed parties.

The professional framing: each standard carries its own written definition, but the common elements are a willing buyer and a willing seller, both reasonably informed, neither under compulsion, the property exposed to the market for a reasonable time, and payment on normal terms. That definition matters because it excludes things a developer often wants included: a buyer who would pay extra for a special reason, a price propped up by unusual seller financing, or a distressed sale. If a lender's loan agreement uses a different defined value, such as liquidation value or a value on a particular basis, the agreement's definition governs that loan. Read the definition the report uses, and verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Intended use and intended user

Plain English: every appraisal is written for someone and for something, and it may not be safe to use for anything else.

The professional framing: the report states its intended use — for example, to support a lending decision — and its intended user, such as a named bank. The scope of work, meaning how much research and analysis was done, is shaped by that use. A desktop opinion prepared for your own internal decision is not a lending appraisal, even if it shows the same number.

Worked example, hypothetical. You commissioned a valuation of your land for your own acquisition decision. Six months later you hand it to a construction lender. The lender declines to use it. This is not personal. The lender was not the intended user, the effective date is stale, and most lenders will order their own appraisal through their own panel to protect independence. If you want to give a lender the benefit of a report you paid for, the usual mechanism is a reliance letter from the appraiser, extending reliance to that lender. Whether one is available, and on what terms, is the appraiser's decision and a matter for your lawyer.

Say that out loud now.

Assumptions that change the meaning of the number

Plain English: some appraisals deliberately assume something that is not true, or not yet known, and the value is only valid if that assumption holds.

The professional framing uses two terms you should recognise from the USPAP family. A hypothetical condition is something the appraiser knows is contrary to fact on the effective date but assumes for the purpose of analysis — for example, that a building not yet built is complete. Every as-complete value rests on a hypothetical condition. An extraordinary assumption is something uncertain on the effective date which, if false, could change the opinion — for example, that a pending rezoning will be approved, or that a soil report not yet received will show normal conditions.

Worked example, hypothetical. A report shows as-is land value of $3,000,000 and, on the next page, $4,500,000 subject to an extraordinary assumption that the site is rezoned for higher density. A developer quotes the $4,500,000 figure in an investor memo without the condition. That is the kind of omission that becomes a misrepresentation argument later. The rule of practice is simple: wherever you quote a conditional value, quote the condition beside it, in the same sentence.

Dates

Every appraisal carries an effective date, the date the value applies to, and a report date, when it was signed. A prospective value, such as as-complete, has an effective date in the future. A value is evidence about one date only. Market conditions after the effective date are not in it.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is pressuring an appraiser. Many jurisdictions and most lenders treat appraiser independence seriously, and some have specific rules forbidding a borrower or a lender's sales staff from influencing the outcome. Even where no rule applies, pressure destroys the value of the opinion and can expose you. The control: communicate with the appraiser only through the channel the lender permits, provide facts and documents, never a target number, and keep a written record of everything you supplied. Professional sign-off required: a designated appraiser for the report, and legal counsel on reliance and on any use in offering documents.

The beginner's mistake

Reading the value on page one and skipping the assumptions and limiting conditions at the back. The back of the report is where the appraiser tells you what the number is not. Read it first.

Callback

In Ford's lesson on Stuyvesant Town, the value depended on a future the rules had not yet allowed. An extraordinary assumption is how a professional report makes that dependency visible. The discipline Ford's rule asks of you — separate today's value from future value — is already built into a well-written appraisal. Your job is to keep that separation when you repeat the number to anyone else.

Recap

Appraisals follow written standards such as USPAP, the Canadian standards, the International Valuation Standards and the Red Book. Each report has an intended use and an intended user, and reliance by anyone else needs a mechanism such as a reliance letter. As-complete values rest on hypothetical conditions; uncertain facts become extraordinary assumptions. Quote conditions with the number, and never pressure an appraiser.

Next: Sage, working backward from a finished appraisal to the rent it requires.
checklist: Read the assumptions and limiting conditions before the value.
Confirm the intended use and intended user match your purpose.
Note the effective date and the report date separately.
List every hypothetical condition and extraordinary assumption.
Quote any conditional value with its condition in the same sentence.
Supply facts and documents to appraisers, never a target number.
Ask counsel before using a report for anyone other than its intended user.
head: Field checklist
speak: An appraisal is a regulated professional opinion. In the United States it follows USPAP; in Canada, the Canadian standards; internationally, the International Valuation Standards or the RICS Red Book, and I verify the current edition before citing any rule. Every report names an intended use and an intended user, and anyone else relying on it usually needs a reliance letter. Dates matter: the effective date is when the value applies. Assumptions matter most. An as-complete value rests on a hypothetical condition, that a building not yet built is finished. An extraordinary assumption is an uncertain fact, like a pending rezoning, that would change the value if false. Whenever I quote a conditional value, I quote the condition in the same sentence. And I never pressure an appraiser. I give facts and documents through the lender's channel, never a target number.
terms: Intended user — the party an appraisal is written for and who is entitled to rely on it.
Hypothetical condition — a condition the appraiser knows is contrary to fact on the effective date but assumes for analysis, such as a building being complete.
Extraordinary assumption — an uncertain fact assumed true on the effective date which, if false, could change the value.

hostile.q: Your investor memo quotes a land value of four and a half million. Where in the appraisal is that number unconditional?
hostile.a: It is not unconditional, and the memo should say so. The appraisal shows three million as-is and four and a half million subject to an extraordinary assumption that the rezoning is approved. I will correct the memo today so both figures and the condition appear together, and I will circulate the correction to everyone who received the original.

title: Working Backward from an Appraised Value to the Rent It Requires
summary: Start with a finished appraisal and reverse the arithmetic: from value to the net operating income it implies, to the gross rent per apartment, and then test that rent against the market. Then check the same value against comparable sales and against cost. Three backward calculations tell you whether a number is credible.
body:
Mr Shabazz, every appraised value quietly asserts a rent. Reverse the arithmetic and you can see that rent in dollars per apartment per month, and test it against what tenants actually pay.

Recall

Q. From this week's first lesson: what are the three approaches to value?

A. The income approach, which asks what the property earns; the sales comparison approach, which asks what similar properties sold for; and the cost approach, which asks what it would cost to build again.

Q. From the second pro forma week: what is the path from potential gross income to net operating income?

A. Potential gross income, less vacancy and credit loss, gives effective gross income. Less operating expenses gives net operating income, before debt service and income tax.

Q. From the week on protecting the base: why keep an emergency reserve outside your business?

A. So a problem in the business does not force you into a personal decision under pressure, and a personal problem does not force a business sale.

Why this matters

You will be handed finished numbers far more often than you build them: a broker's valuation, a lender's appraisal, a seller's asking price. Working forward requires all the inputs. Working backward requires only the answer and a few market ratios, and it exposes the assumption carrying the conclusion. This is an even-numbered week, so we start from the outcome and walk back. Every number below is hypothetical. The skill takes five minutes with a calculator, and once you have done it a dozen times you will do the first two steps in your head while the broker is still talking.

The outcome we start from

An appraisal for a new 80-apartment building states an as-stabilised value of $20,000,000, using direct capitalisation at a cap rate of 5.75 percent. The developer's total cost, including land, is $18,000,000. That is all we are given. We will use two market ratios that you would confirm locally: vacancy and credit loss of 5 percent of potential gross income, and operating expenses of 35 percent of effective gross income.

Step 1: From value back to NOI

Value equals net operating income divided by cap rate, so NOI equals value times cap rate.

$20,000,000 times 0.0575 equals $1,150,000 of stabilised NOI per year.

Step 2: From NOI back to effective gross income

If operating expenses are 35 percent of effective gross income (EGI), NOI is the remaining 65 percent. So EGI equals NOI divided by 0.65.

$1,150,000 divided by 0.65 equals about $1,769,000 of EGI per year.

Step 3: From EGI back to potential gross income

If vacancy and credit loss take 5 percent of potential gross income (PGI), EGI is 95 percent of it. So PGI equals EGI divided by 0.95.

$1,769,000 divided by 0.95 equals about $1,862,000 of PGI per year.

Say that out loud now.

Step 4: From PGI back to rent per apartment

Divide by the number of apartments, then by twelve months. If the building has other income such as parking, subtract it first; here we assume none.

  • $1,862,000 divided by 80 apartments equals about $23,280 per apartment per year.
  • $23,280 divided by 12 equals about $1,940 per apartment per month.

That is the claim the appraisal is making: this building will achieve an average of about $1,940 per apartment per month, with 5 percent vacancy and a 35 percent expense ratio, and buyers will capitalise it at 5.75 percent.

Step 5: Test the implied rent

Now compare $1,940 with evidence. Suppose current listings for comparable new apartments in the area average $1,800, and recent leases in the newest competing building average $1,850. The appraisal needs rents about 5 percent above the best current evidence. That is not automatically wrong; a better building or a rising market may justify it. But it is now a specific question you can put to the appraiser: which rent comparables support $1,940?

And it has a price. Rerun Step 1 to Step 4 forward at $1,850: PGI is $1,850 times 12 times 80, or $1,776,000. EGI is 95 percent, $1,687,200. NOI is 65 percent, about $1,096,700. Value at 5.75 percent is about $19,073,000. A $90 difference in monthly rent is worth about $927,000 of value.

Cross-check 1: Sales comparison

$20,000,000 divided by 80 apartments equals $250,000 per apartment. If recent sales of comparable new buildings fall between $230,000 and $245,000 per apartment, the income approach is sitting above the top of the sales evidence. Two approaches now point the same way, which strengthens the question.

Cross-check 2: Cost and the development spread

Divide the implied NOI by the developer's total cost to get yield on cost: $1,150,000 divided by $18,000,000 equals about 6.39 percent. Compare that with the 5.75 percent cap rate. The spread is about 0.64 percentage points, or 64 basis points. Value of $20,000,000 against cost of $18,000,000 also implies a profit of $2,000,000, about 11 percent of cost. Whether 64 basis points and 11 percent are enough reward for the risk is a judgement; the commercial norms vary by market and cycle and are not standards. But you now know the size of the cushion, and that a rent shortfall of $90 a month consumes almost half of it.

Cross-check 3: The rent at which the profit disappears

One more backward step, and it is the one I would put on the first page of any memo. Ask what rent makes value exactly equal to cost, so that the developer's profit is zero. Value equal to $18,000,000 at a 5.75 percent cap rate requires NOI of $18,000,000 times 0.0575, which is $1,035,000. NOI is 65 percent of EGI, and EGI is 95 percent of PGI, so NOI is 0.65 times 0.95, or 61.75 percent, of PGI. PGI is therefore $1,035,000 divided by 0.6175, about $1,676,000. Divided by 80 apartments and 12 months, that is about $1,746 per apartment per month.

So the deal has a rent cushion of about $194 a month between the appraisal's $1,940 and break-even at $1,746, about 10 percent. Against current evidence of $1,850, the real cushion is only about $104, under 6 percent. That one sentence — "rents can fall 6 percent from today's evidence before the profit is gone" — tells an investor more than the appraised value ever will. It also assumes the cap rate holds; if it rises, the break-even rent rises with it.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is accepting a value without ever seeing the rent it requires. Values are quoted in millions; tenants pay in hundreds. The control is to reverse every value you are given into rent per apartment per month, and into price per apartment, and to put both beside current evidence before you discuss the value at all.

The beginner's mistake

Reversing with the wrong ratios. If you assume a 30 percent expense ratio where the building really runs at 40 percent, your backward rent will look comfortably low and you will approve a value you should have questioned. The backward method is only as good as the market ratios you feed it, so source them from comparable buildings, not from the appraisal you are testing.

Callback

In the value week you learned that a development spread is yield on cost minus the market cap rate. Here you met it in reverse: from an appraised value back to an implied NOI, then forward to a yield on cost. The same spread, reached from the other direction, gives you a second way to check any deal you are shown.

Recap

From an as-stabilised value of $20,000,000 at a 5.75 percent cap rate, we reversed to NOI of $1,150,000, EGI of about $1,769,000, PGI of about $1,862,000, and an implied rent of about $1,940 per apartment per month. Against evidence of $1,850, that rent is worth about $927,000 of value. Price per apartment and yield on cost gave two independent cross-checks.

Next: Roman, in the room when the appraisal comes in low.
checklist: Reverse every value to NOI using the stated cap rate.
Source the expense ratio and vacancy from comparable buildings, not the report.
Reverse NOI to effective gross income, then to potential gross income.
Remove other income before calculating rent per apartment.
Express the result in rent per apartment per month.
Compare the implied rent with current listings and recent leases.
Cross-check price per apartment against comparable sales.
Calculate yield on cost and the spread over the cap rate.
head: Field checklist
speak: Every value asserts a rent, and I can reverse it. Take an as-stabilised value of twenty million at a five point seven five percent cap rate. NOI is value times cap rate: one point one five million. If operating expenses take thirty-five percent of effective gross income, NOI is sixty-five percent of it, so effective gross is about one point seven seven million. If vacancy is five percent, potential gross is about one point eight six million. Divide by eighty apartments and twelve months: about one thousand nine hundred and forty dollars a month. Then I test that rent against evidence. If the best comparables lease at one eight five zero, the appraisal needs about five percent more, and that ninety dollars is worth about nine hundred thousand of value. I cross-check price per apartment against sales, and yield on cost against the cap rate.
terms: Effective gross income — potential gross income less vacancy and credit loss, plus any other income actually collected.
Potential gross income — the total rent a property would earn if every unit were leased at market rent all year.
Basis point — one hundredth of one percentage point; 64 basis points is 0.64 percentage points.

hostile.q: Your appraisal implies rents five percent above anything leasing in the area today. What supports that?
hostile.a: I reversed it myself and see the same five percent. Our support is that the unit mix and finishes exceed the newest competitor, but I do not want the loan to rest on that. Here is the deal sized at today's best evidence of eighteen fifty: value falls by about nine hundred thousand, the loan is still covered, and our equity reserve absorbs the difference.

title: In the Room When the Appraisal Comes In Low
summary: A low appraisal is a negotiation over evidence, not over a number. This scene walks through a call with a lender's credit officer, with the lines to say, the lines never to say, the question behind the question, when to stay silent, and how to hold your state. It closes with a note on working with advisers.
body:
Mr Shabazz, when an appraisal comes in low, the meeting is not about the number. It is about whether you respond with evidence or with pressure, and the lender decides what kind of borrower you are within the first two minutes.

Recall

Q. From this week's failure forensics: what did Rule 16 say?

A. Value what exists under today's rules first; any value that depends on a future change must be financed with equity and time, never borrowed against as if it were already earned.

Q. From the second pro forma week: what is lease-up?

A. The period from first occupancy to stabilisation, during which income rises as units are leased and the owner usually carries a shortfall.

Q. From the week on protecting the base: who should know where your key documents are?

A. The people you have appointed to act for you, so that if you cannot act, someone can find the will, the insurance and the account details without delay.

Why this matters

You will have this conversation. Values are opinions, and sooner or later one will come in below your plan at a moment when land is bought and contractors are waiting. How you handle the first call decides whether the lender sees a disciplined borrower with a problem, or a problem with a borrower attached. The same habits apply with a buyer's appraisal at sale and an investor's valuation review.

The scene

This is a composite example, with hypothetical numbers. You are developing a 40-unit building. Your plan assumed an as-complete value of $12,000,000. The lender's appraisal, ordered through its own panel, concludes $10,800,000. At the lender's maximum of 60 percent of value, the loan falls from your expected $6,500,000 to $6,480,000 — small — but the lender's credit officer also flags that the appraiser's rent conclusion is $1,800 a month against your $1,950. That second fact is the real issue, because it touches debt service coverage once the building is leased. The credit officer, whom we will call Dana, opens the call: "We have the appraisal. It is below your number. Walk me through where you think it is wrong."

Lines to say

  • "Thank you for sending it early. Before I say anything about the number, can I confirm I understand the appraiser's rent and cap rate conclusions?" This shows you read it and you are not about to argue from emotion.
  • "The cap rate I agree with. The difference is the rent conclusion, $1,800 against our $1,950. I have three leases from the newest comparable building that I believe the appraiser did not have. May I send them to you so you can decide whether they go to the appraiser?" Evidence, through the lender's channel, with the lender deciding.
  • "If the rent conclusion stands, here is what the deal looks like at $1,800." Then give the numbers you prepared before the call.
  • "I will send the leases and the revised case by Thursday at noon." A specific time, kept.

Say that out loud now.

Notice what those four lines do together. They separate the parts of the appraisal you accept from the one part you dispute, they keep the lender in control of the process, and they put a fallback on the table before anyone has asked for it. A credit officer writes a note after every call. You want hers to read: "Borrower accepts cap rate, disputes rent with new evidence, and has shown the deal works at our number."

Lines never to say

  • "Can you get the appraiser to twelve?" That is a request to influence an independent opinion. Many lenders treat it as a serious problem, and in some contexts it can breach rules on appraiser independence.
  • "Other banks would have come in higher." It insults the lender and tells them you are shopping for a number rather than a truth.
  • "The appraiser does not understand this market." Perhaps true, but unprovable on a call and it sounds like a man who has run out of evidence.
  • "We need this to close by Friday or the deal dies." Urgency transfers your problem to the lender and invites a worse term.

The question behind the question

Dana asked where the appraisal is wrong. The question behind it is: "If the appraiser is right, does this borrower still survive?" A credit officer has to defend the loan to a committee that will assume the lower number is correct. Your job is to make that defence easy. So the most powerful thing you can bring is not an argument that the appraisal is wrong, but a prepared case showing the project works at the appraiser's figures. Here is that worked example. At $1,800 a month, 40 units earn $864,000 of potential gross income a year. Less 5 percent vacancy, $820,800. Less 35 percent expenses, NOI of about $533,500. If annual debt service on the loan is $420,000, coverage is $533,500 divided by $420,000, about 1.27 times. If the lender's minimum is 1.25, a figure that is commercial practice and varies by lender, you still pass, narrowly. Lead with that.

When to stay silent

Twice. After you ask whether you have understood the appraiser's conclusions, stop and let Dana answer fully; she may tell you which point the committee cares about. And after you present the at-the-appraisal case, stop. The silence after a strong number does more work than any sentence you could add to it.

Holding your state

A low number lands as a threat, and the body responds before the mind does: the voice rises and speeds up. Before the call, while you are parked and not driving, take a few slow breaths with a longer exhale, and say the first sentence aloud once. On the call, slow your pace on purpose and keep your sentences short. If you feel heat, write the next number down before you say it. If you have any health concern about stress responses, check that with your doctor.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is turning a valuation disagreement into a relationship problem. Lenders remember borrowers who pressured appraisers long after they forget the number. The control is a rule you set before the call: you will offer evidence and a solution, never a target, and every document you supply goes through the lender.

The beginner's mistake

Arguing every adjustment. A beginner disputes ten points, so the one point that matters, the rent conclusion, is lost among nine weak ones. Choose the single largest, best-evidenced difference and let the rest go.

Working with advisers

This month's thread is working with advisers, and an appraisal is a good place to start. The advisers you hire — appraisers, lawyers, accountants, engineers — are most valuable when they are free to tell you what you do not want to hear. If you only ever reward agreement, you will gradually be surrounded by people who have learned to agree.

A practical habit: when you engage an adviser, write down in one paragraph what decision their work will inform and what answer would change your mind. Then read their conclusion against that paragraph, not against your hope. It turns an adviser's report from a hurdle into an instrument.

Callback

In this week's lesson on the rules behind an appraisal, REGA warned that pressuring an appraiser destroys the value of the opinion. This scene is what that rule looks like in practice: evidence through the lender's channel, the lender deciding what reaches the appraiser, and a solution prepared at the appraiser's own figures.

Recap

Confirm you understand the conclusions, isolate the one difference that matters, offer evidence through the lender, show the deal working at the appraiser's number, then stay silent. Never ask for a target, never threaten a deadline, never insult the appraiser. Prepare your state before the call, while parked.

Next: Kema, with the week's six questions and Cole's Auditor's Chair.
checklist: Read the full appraisal before the call, including assumptions.
Prepare a case showing the deal at the appraiser's own figures.
Choose the single largest, best-evidenced difference.
Send new evidence through the lender, never directly to the appraiser.
Never name a target value.
Commit to a specific time for any follow-up, and keep it.
Prepare your opening sentence aloud while parked, not driving.
head: Field checklist
speak: When an appraisal comes in low, I treat it as a question about evidence, not a fight about a number. I confirm I understand the appraiser's rent and cap rate conclusions. I isolate the one difference that matters most, for example rent of eighteen hundred against my nineteen fifty. I offer new evidence through the lender, and let the lender decide whether it goes to the appraiser. Then I show the deal working at the appraiser's own figure: at eighteen hundred a month, forty units give NOI of about five hundred and thirty thousand, and coverage of about one point two seven times. Then I stop talking. I never ask anyone to hit a number, never threaten a deadline, never insult the appraiser. The credit officer's real question is whether I survive if the appraiser is right, so I answer that question first.
terms: Debt service coverage ratio — net operating income divided by annual debt payments; lenders set a minimum as commercial practice.
Appraiser independence — the principle that the appraiser's opinion must not be influenced by the borrower or by anyone paid on the loan closing.
Credit committee — the lender's internal body that approves loans, to which the credit officer must defend each one.

hostile.q: If our appraiser is right about rent, your coverage is barely above our minimum. Why should we not cut the loan further?
hostile.a: Because at the appraiser's rent the loan still clears your minimum, and I am not asking you to rely on my rent. If you want more margin, I would rather add an interest reserve funded with our equity than reduce the loan, which keeps your coverage protected through lease-up without changing the structure.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Valuation Week Review: Six Questions and the Auditor's Chair
summary: Six questions test the week on valuation: the three approaches, as-is against as-complete value, appraisal assumptions, and how value moves debt and equity. Cole's Auditor's Chair reads a hypothetical appraisal summary the way a hostile auditor would. A two-minute boardroom drill closes the week.
body:
Mr Shabazz, this week taught one idea from six angles: value is an opinion with a structure, and you can test that structure without becoming an appraiser. Today we check that it stuck.

Recall

Q. From this week's money lesson: what is the binding limit on a loan?

A. Whichever of the lender's sizing tests produces the smallest loan, such as loan-to-cost or loan-to-value. That test sets the loan.

Q. From the second pro forma week: what makes NOI "stabilised"?

A. It is measured after lease-up, once occupancy has settled at a sustainable level, with normal vacancy and expenses included.

Q. From the week on protecting the base: what is the difference between a reserve and an investment?

A. A reserve exists to be available when something goes wrong, so it is held for safety and access, not for return.

Why this matters

Valuation sits underneath every loan you will take and every sale you will make. If you can only repeat a value, others will set your leverage for you. If you can take it apart, you can negotiate from evidence.

The six questions

Question 1. Name the three approaches to value and where each one bends.

Answer: The income approach bends at the cap rate and at how honestly net operating income was normalised. The sales comparison approach bends at the adjustments to each comparable. The cost approach bends at depreciation, which is why it is strongest for new buildings.

Question 2. What is the difference between as-is and as-complete value?

Answer: As-is is the value of the property in its current physical and legal condition on the valuation date. As-complete is a forward-looking value that assumes, as a hypothetical condition, that the planned building is finished.

Question 3. What is an extraordinary assumption, and what must you do when you quote a value that rests on one?

Answer: It is an uncertain fact, assumed true on the effective date, that would change the value if false — a pending rezoning, for example. Whenever you quote that value, quote the assumption in the same sentence.

Question 4. A lender lends 65 percent of a $10,000,000 cost and 60 percent of appraised value. The appraisal is $10,000,000. What is the loan and the equity?

Answer: The cost test gives $6,500,000 and the value test gives $6,000,000. The smaller binds, so the loan is $6,000,000 and the equity is $4,000,000.

Question 5. An appraisal shows value of $20,000,000 at a 5.75 percent cap rate. What NOI does it imply?

Answer: Value times cap rate: $1,150,000 a year.

Question 6. What is Rule 16?

Answer: Value what exists under today's rules first; any value that depends on a future change must be financed with equity and time, never borrowed against as if it were already earned.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

Sage gave you the three approaches and the insight that the gap between income value and cost is why development happens. Ford showed, through Stuyvesant Town, what happens when price and debt rest on a future the rules have not permitted. Priya showed how appraised value sets the loan, the equity and the return, and how leverage magnifies a change in value. REGA gave you the standards, the intended user and the two kinds of conditional assumption. Sage reversed a value into the rent it requires. Roman put you in the room with a low appraisal.

Cole's Auditor's Chair

Every fourth week the Red Pen becomes Cole's Auditor's Chair: you read a hypothetical document as a hostile auditor would, looking for what is missing, inconsistent or convenient. Here is the summary page of a hypothetical appraisal, reproduced in a developer's investor memo.

"Valuation summary. Intended user: the developer. Effective date: fourteen months before the memo. Market value as-complete: $15,000,000. Income approach: stabilised NOI of $900,000 at a cap rate of 6.0 percent, derived from recent sales of suburban office buildings. Sales comparison approach: three sales averaging $260,000 per unit, adjusted upward 5 percent each for location, size, finishes and market conditions. Cost approach: land $3,000,000 plus construction cost $11,000,000, no depreciation, total $14,000,000. Reconciled value: the average of the three approaches. The rezoning of the site to residential use has been assumed."

Read it once more as the auditor. Then compare with the defects below.

  1. The intended user is the developer, not the lender or the investors who are reading it. Nobody else may be entitled to rely on it.
  2. The effective date is fourteen months old. Market conditions since then are not in the number.
  3. The income arithmetic works — $900,000 divided by 0.06 is $15,000,000 — but the cap rate comes from suburban office sales, a different property type with different tenants, risks and buyers. The income approach, the one that carries the conclusion, rests on the wrong evidence.
  4. Four upward adjustments of 5 percent each, all in one direction, quietly lift the comparables by about 20 percent.
  5. The cost approach carries no entrepreneurial incentive, so it understates what a developer would need, and "no depreciation" is only reasonable for a new building — the memo does not say the building is new.
  6. Reconciliation by simple average is not reconciliation. The appraiser should weigh each approach by the strength of its evidence.
  7. The rezoning is an extraordinary assumption, stated last and not beside the value. The as-is value under current zoning is missing entirely.

The auditor's conclusion would be blunt: this summary cannot support an investment decision until it is reissued to the right intended user, brought up to date, and shows the as-is value beside the conditional one.

The boardroom drill

Stand up, set a two-minute timer, and explain valuation to a board as if they have never heard the word cap rate. Then compare with the model answer.

Model answer: "A valuation is a professional opinion of the price a property would fetch in a fair sale. It is built three ways. The income approach divides stabilised net operating income by a cap rate; it is most sensitive to that cap rate. The sales approach adjusts recent comparable sales. The cost approach adds land to the cost of building new, less depreciation. A good appraiser weighs them by the evidence. For us, valuation matters because the lender sizes the loan partly on it, so a low appraisal raises our equity, and at sale a small move in cap rate moves our equity by a much larger percentage. Our discipline is three things. We separate today's value from any value that depends on a future approval. We reverse every value into the rent it requires and test that rent against the market. And we never pressure an appraiser; we bring evidence through the lender."

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is forgetting it under pressure: quoting a conditional value without its condition at the moment you most need the money. The control is to keep a one-line habit in every document you sign: value, basis, date, conditions.

The beginner's mistake

Studying the approaches and skipping the reversing. You will rarely build an appraisal from scratch, but you will be handed finished values every week — by brokers, sellers, lenders and partners. The reversing is the skill you will use weekly: value to NOI, NOI to rent per apartment per month, then a look at what tenants actually pay. Practise it until the first two steps happen in your head.

Callback

In the returns week, Sage and Elias warned that a return quoted before tax can mislead. A value quoted without its conditions misleads the same way: the headline is true in one narrow sense and false for the decision being made.

Recap

Three approaches, two kinds of conditional assumption, one binding limit, one reversed rent, and one rule. Practise the boardroom drill aloud once more before you close the app.

head: The six questions
speak: This week was valuation. There are three approaches. Income: net operating income divided by a cap rate, sensitive to that cap rate. Sales comparison: recent sales adjusted for differences, sensitive to the adjustments. Cost: land plus the cost of building new, less depreciation, best for new buildings. A good appraiser weighs them by evidence, not by averaging. As-is value is the property today; as-complete assumes the building is finished, a hypothetical condition. An extraordinary assumption, like a pending rezoning, must be quoted beside any value that rests on it. Lenders lend the smaller of a share of cost and a share of value, so a low appraisal raises my equity, and leverage magnifies any fall in value. I reverse every value into the rent it requires and test that rent against the market. Rule 16: value what exists under today's rules first, and finance future upside with equity and time.
terms: Auditor's Chair — Cole's drill of reading a document as a hostile auditor would, looking for what is missing, stale or convenient.
Effective date — the date on which an appraised value applies, separate from the date the report was signed.
Entrepreneurial incentive — the allowance for developer profit added in the cost approach to reflect the reward needed to take on the risk of building.

hostile.q: Your memo averages three valuation approaches and cites an appraisal written for you, fourteen months ago, that assumes a rezoning. What exactly are investors being asked to rely on?
hostile.a: As written, nothing they are entitled to rely on, and I will withdraw that page. I will commission an updated appraisal addressed to the investors and the lender, show the as-is value under current zoning beside the value assuming rezoning, and have the appraiser reconcile the approaches by the weight of evidence rather than by average.
